verses.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy to them,

and say, ‘You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord Yahweh! Thus says the Lord Yahweh to the mountains and to the hills, to the watercourses and to the valleys: “Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword on you, and I will destroy your high places.
Your altars will become desolate, and your incense altars will be broken. I will cast down your slain men before your idols.
I will lay the dead bodies of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones around your altars.

In all your dwelling places the cities shall be laid waste, and the high places shall be desolate; that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your incense altars may be cut down, and your works may be abolished.
The slain shall fall among you, and you shall know that I am Yahweh.
“‘“Yet I will leave a remnant, in that you will have some that escape the sword among the nations, when you are scattered through the countries.

Those of you that escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken with their lewd heart, which has departed from me, and with their eyes, which play the prostitute after their idols. Then they will loathe themselves in their own sight for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations.
They will know that I am Yahweh. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them.”’

“Thus says the Lord Yahweh: ‘Strike with your hand, and stamp with your foot, and say, “Alas!” Because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel; for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence.
He who is far off will die of the pestilence. He who is near will fall by the sword. He who remains and is besieged will die by the famine. Thus I will accomplish my wrath on them.

You will know that I am Yahweh, when their slain men are among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the tops of the mountains, under every green tree, and under every thick oak, the places where they offered pleasant aroma to all their idols.
I will stretch out my hand on them, and make the land desolate and waste, from the wilderness toward Diblah, throughout all their habitations: and they will know that I am Yahweh. ’”

footnotes.content: When the Lord speaks, a prophet listens. Ezekiel has already seen visions that shook him to his bones—wheels within wheels, creatures of fire. Now comes the word itself: a call to turn and speak judgment. Before we can carry hard truth, we must first hear it ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Set your face toward the mountains." The prophet's body language matters—feet planted, gaze fixed. This is not a passing comment but a proclamation with weight behind it. To speak for God, we stand firm, our very posture a sign that we have seen something the world has not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High places were Israel's false shrines, the work of human pride. God addresses even the land itself—mountains and valleys—as if all creation is listening. When we build altars to ourselves rather than to the Lord, even the earth knows it. Grace comes as judgment first, that we might turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The idols will fall, their altars torn down. There is something merciful here, hard as it sounds: the Lord will not permit His people to keep bowing to stone and wood forever. Sometimes love breaks what we cling to so that we might cling to Him instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stark image—the slain before the idols, bones scattered. This speaks to a people so turned from God that judgment reaches them in the places where they sought false comfort. Yet even this horror is the Lord calling, "Remember me. See that your way leads nowhere."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Desolation in all dwelling places. The prophecy spans every level: the city, the shrine, the altar. Nowhere is spared because the turning-away from God was not partial—it was thorough. When we imagine ourselves safe in half-truth, judgment touches every refuge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall know that I am Yahweh." This refrain echoes through Ezekiel: the Lord is not hidden, not silent, not powerless. Even in devastation, Israel will know His name. That knowing is the beginning of restoration, for a people who have forgotten Him can only be healed when they remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A door opens in the darkness—"I will leave a remnant." Even as the sword falls, grace reserves some to escape. The Lord's arm of judgment has never been meant to end all things, but to purify, to preserve a seed from which faith can grow again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Scattered among the nations, the remnant remembers. And remembrance begins with shame—they loathe the idolatry, the spiritual whoredom their fathers embraced. Repentance is not easy, but it is possible. In exile and sorrow, the Lord reaches the hearts of those who will turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have not said in vain." The Lord's word will not return empty. What is promised—whether grace or judgment—will surely come to pass. This is both warning and comfort: if the Lord has spoken judgment, it will stand; if He has promised renewal, He will keep it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strike your hand, stamp your foot, cry "Alas!" The prophet's lament is embodied, physical. This is not detached sermon but the groaning of one who sees what his people have done and knows the cost. True prophetic word carries weight in the body, the voice, the soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No escape route: distance brings pestilence, nearness brings the sword, and those who hide face famine. This is not random cruelty but the exhaustion of mercy when a people have refused to turn. The Lord does not take pleasure in it, but His justice will be done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High hills, green trees, thick oaks—sacred groves where fertility gods were worshipped, places of secret sin. The Lord names each place where His people forsook Him. But knowing itself is already the threshold of return. God remembers what we do in shadow; He calls us home by that memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land laid waste from wilderness to Diblah—a judgment that seemed final. Yet readers today hear an echo: even desolation need not be the end. The God who stretches out His hand to destroy can stretch it out to restore. Exile is not the last word when the Lord is speaking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
